title: Service Onboarding Runway and SLO Admission Playbook
author: Anya Patel
body:
Summary:
This playbook defines a standardized process for bringing a new inference service (model or feature) into production at Redwood Inference. It codifies the notion of a "capacity runway" — the validated buffer of provisioned capacity and mitigations that allow safe growth — and the SLO admission checks the SRE team requires before granting a full production SLA. Use this playbook for new tenant onboarding, major model upgrades, and feature launches that materially change traffic or tail-latency characteristics.

Goals:
- Ensure new services enter production with measurable SLOs, telemetry, and an explicit capacity runway.
- Prevent noisy or untested workloads from consuming shared capacity without staged validation.
- Provide a repeatable set of gates and ownership steps for steering teams and SRE reviewers.

Audience:
- Product and ML engineers (service owners)
- SRE reviewers and capacity planners
- Platform engineers enabling autoscaling and admission controls

Quick definitions:
- Capacity runway: validated provisioned headroom (expressed as GPU-minutes or qps-equivalent) plus mitigation controls (rate limits, throttles, fallback models) that allow a service to absorb growth for a defined horizon (default 14 days).
- SLO admission: a checklist of observability, isolation, and performance criteria required to move a service from "staging" to "production".
- Admit token: short-lived flag granted by SRE that enables full routing to production endpoints.

Admission gates (must pass all):
1) Observability and telemetry
   - Request traces and spans instrumented end-to-end (client -> router -> runtime). Example: trace parent header propagated and visible in /traces for 100% of sampled requests.
   - Per-route counters collected: requests, successes, failures (4xx/5xx), token_count, kv_cache_hit, average_inflight.
   - Request-level latency histograms with p50/p90/p95/p99.99 buckets.
   - Synthetic canaries configured and running: two synthetic scenarios that reflect production traffic patterns and edge cases.
   - Telemetry retention: 90 days for aggregated metrics, 30 days for traces by default (longer retention requires business approval).

2) SLOs defined and tested
   - Define availability SLO (example default: 99.95% for hosted API route, 99.9% for dedicated customers unless contracted).
   - Define latency SLOs: p95 < X ms and p99 < Y ms where X/Y are service-specific — suggest default for small prompt routes: p95 < 250ms, p99 < 600ms.
   - Error budget policy: a burn-rate ladder (see "Error budget thresholds" section).
   - Acceptance test: run 72-hour synthetic workload at 2x expected steady-state qps and verify SLOs and cache/kv behavior.

3) Capacity runway and isolation
   - Minimum runway: sufficient capacity to sustain 7 days at 2x expected qps and absorb 3x expected burst for 5 minutes without violating the SLO. Default: 14-day runway recommended for public endpoints.
   - Isolation features: tenant priority tags, token-level throttles, and pre-warmed pools for heavy models.
   - Autoscaling policy exists and is validated in a staging environment with at least three scale cycles (cold->warm->scale-down).

4) Throttles, fallbacks, and graceful degradation
   - Circuit breakers configured: per-tenant rate limit, global route fallback, and model-variant fallback.
   - Fallback behavior documented: when quantized or smaller-variant model is used, latency and quality impact communicated.
   - Backpressure signals: 429/503 mapping and consumer guidance included in API docs.

5) Security and compliance checks
   - Data residency and encryption meet customer contractual requirements.
   - Audit logging enabled for admin actions and model version rollouts.

SRE admission checklist (concrete steps)
1) Service owner fills onboarding form (reference template) including expected qps, 95/99 latency targets, model details, expected token mix, and requested SLA.
2) Run local synthetic smoke tests against staging cluster and upload artifacts (charts, raw histograms).
3) SRE performs a telemetry validation pass: ensure all metrics and traces are present.
4) Capacity planner simulates load with the service's expected traffic pattern and validates runway calculations.
5) If runway insufficient, agree on mitigations (reserved capacity, initial hard quota, or reduced rollout).
6) On successful validation, SRE grants an admit token with explicit expiry (default 30 days) and documents the status in the onboarding tracker.

Error budget thresholds and automated signals
- Normal: burn rate <= 1.0 — no action.
- Elevated: 1.0 < burn rate <= 3.0 — SRE/owner notification; increase synthetic tests cadence; consider temporary throttle increases.
- Critical: burn rate > 3.0 for > 15 minutes — automatic admission freeze, shift traffic to fallback route, SRE paged (P1).
- Escalation policy: sustained critical (> 1 hour) triggers incident bridge and postmortem.

Capacity runway formula (reference)
- Inputs: expected_qps, avg_tokens_per_request, baseline_cost_per_token (gpu-time-equivalent), target_runway_days, safety_multiplier.
- Simplified runway (GPU-minutes equiv) = expected_qps * avg_tokens * baseline_cost_per_token * 60 * 60 * 24 * target_runway_days * safety_multiplier.
- Example: expected_qps=10, avg_tokens=100, baseline_cost=0.0003 GPU-min/token, target=14 days, safety=1.25 -> runway ≈ 10*100*0.0003*86400*14*1.25 ≈ 45360 GPU-minutes (this is an example; use the capacity calculator spreadsheet for exact mapping to instance counts).

Runbook: immediate remediation when runway stress detected
1) Detect: alert fires when capacity_utilization > 85% for 5m or burst > 95% for 1m.
2) Triage: SRE oncall checks service tag, current admit tokens, and error budget burn rate.
3) Mitigate quickly: a) enforce temporary per-token hard rate limit; b) redirect a percentage of traffic to canary or fallback model; c) scale up reserved pool if autoscaling insufficient and pre-approved budget exists.
4) Restore: once utilization < 70% and burn rate < 1.0 for 30m, remove temporary limits per documented rollback steps.
5) Post-incident: raise a postmortem if mitigation exceeds 30 minutes or SLO breach occurred.

Operational tooling and admission controller
- Admission Controller role: validates metadata from service manifest and computes a provisional capacity footprint. It enforces minimum telemetry, synthetic canaries, and timeline for runway.
- CLI example: redwood admision validate --manifest service.yaml --staging-cluster staging-a
- Manifest snippet (YAML as text):
  service_name: conversational-rewrite
  expected_qps: 8
  avg_tokens: 120
  latency_targets:
    p95_ms: 220
    p99_ms: 550
  canary_tests:
    - name: basic-intent
      qps: 1
      duration_mins: 30

- Policy example (text table):
  | Field | Minimum requirement | Example |
  |-------|---------------------|---------|
  | traces | propagated | yes |
  | metrics | p50/p95/p99 histograms | yes |
  | synthetic | 2 scenarios running | yes |
  | capacity_runway | 14 days recommended | 14 |

Ownership and roles
- Service Owner: responsible for test artifacts, communication plan, and quality regressions.
- SRE Reviewer: performs telemetry and capacity validation and grants admit token.
- Capacity Planner: owns simulation and runway sizing.
- Platform: implements and operates the admission controller and throttling primitives.

Canary and staged rollout guidance
1) Canary: start with 0.5–2% of traffic for 24–48 hours while monitoring SLOs and evasion patterns.
2) Gradual ramp: double traffic slice every 12–24 hours if metrics stable and burn rate <= 1.0.
3) Abort conditions: p99 latency > target by 30% for > 15 minutes, error budget burn rate crosses Critical, or token consumption cost > 2x forecast.

Post-onboarding activities
- Monthly runway review: validate runway against observed qps and update autoscale policies.
- Capacity debt register: if service operates on mitigations (throttles, fallbacks) add entry to the debt register with owner and remediation due date.
- Smoke test cadence: maintain weekly synthetic canaries for 30 days after major model upgrades.

Appendices
A) Example admission manifest (full):
  service_name: "summarize-lite"
  owner: "team-summaries@example.com"
  expected_qps: 12
  peak_factor: 3
  avg_tokens: 80
  runway_days: 14
  synthetic_tests:
    - name: short-docs
      qps: 1
      duration_mins: 60
    - name: adversarial-lengths
      qps: 0.25
      duration_mins: 30

If you are a service owner ready to start onboarding, open the admission form and tag @sre-review in the ticketing system. For urgent capacity concerns during onboarding call the SRE oncall phone per the incident directory.
